html:
The siege of Madrid lasted from November 1936 to 28 March 1939, during the Spanish Civil War. The capital of the Spanish Republic held out against the Nationalist army of Francisco Franco for almost two and a half years, and its surrender ended the war.

The war began in July 1936 when part of the army rose against the elected left-wing government. The rising failed in Madrid, and Franco marched on the city with his troops from Morocco. The government left for Valencia, but on 8 November workers' militias, the first International Brigades, and tanks and aircraft from the Soviet Union stopped the attack in the western suburbs. German and Italian planes bombed the city, one of the first air attacks on a large European capital. Franco gave up the direct assault after two weeks. His attempts to cut the city off in 1937 also failed.

By early 1939 the Republic had lost Catalonia, and Madrid was starving. Officers in the city overthrew the government to seek terms. Franco offered none and marched in unopposed. He ruled Spain until 1975. For Germany, Italy and the Soviet Union the war had been a testing ground for World War II.
